rationale: A wins because it keeps the launch out of press-release cosplay and makes each angle answerable: "The story isn't the agent — it's the number it exposes" is exactly the discipline this update needs. B has usable raw material, but it keeps sneaking unsupported autonomy and market claims into the frame; "The average company wastes $342,000" is not what a 200-company beta proves. The biggest difference is proof hygiene: A asks the questions before a reporter does, while B lets "presumably" carry an entire contrarian angle.
gaps_in_A: "cancels your software subscriptions" overstates the workflow; the update says the agent drafts emails that finance approves, not that it cancels autonomously.
"The first AI agents in finance departments" is an unsupported first-mover claim. Cut "first" unless Ramp can prove it.
"charging for the approval workflow" assumes the enterprise tier is paid; likely, but not stated in the update.
gaps_in_B: "The average company wastes $342,000" turns a 200-company Ramp beta average into a market-wide claim. That is how a data angle gets killed in the first fact-check.

"As Ramp customers, this beta group presumably already had spend visibility" is a premise dressed up as evidence; the update never says the beta companies were existing Ramp customers or had prior spend visibility.
"initiating a real-world business transaction" and "negotiation with an AI agent" overstate autonomy; the facts say the agent drafts emails that finance approves.
"doing part of the procurement analyst's job" drifts toward labor-substitution without headcount, hiring, or role-scope evidence.
